e-5570.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
e-5570.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/8a460dfb89b0d2e9c1e197aa212f494971df1c36822117fb4b1271f5608d1d1a.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/a172f54b0dc879c2363cfd2818fc79614d68662def6dd56b0ac9aec8fdbca1a5.png) Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}.$
e-5570.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{b}\}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2+1\cdot 9+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot (-1)}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{4+9+0-1}{4+1+0+1}b \\  & =\frac{12}{6}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

e-5571.knowledge_point: Calculating the Distance  Between a Vector and a One-Dimensional Subspace
e-5571.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/fb060fbc7ac20ff3b739a7c8958b4977e72abd31679c098973395db99fb6f78e.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/7a20f39cb1c7c36a01e9d7d4dcd8cbe619c8cffacb57bc2bf42b8d46ce53bb5b.png) If $\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{y} + \mathbf{z},$ where $\mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and $\mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},$ then find $\mathbf{z}.$
e-5571.worked_solution:
A diagram of the situation is provided below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 4+(-1)\cdot (-4)+0\cdot 2+(-1)\cdot 2}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{4+4+0-2}{1+1+0+1}a \\  & =\frac{6}{3}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following:  

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $\mathbf{y} \in \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\}$ and $\mathbf{z} \perp \text{Span}\{\mathbf{a}\},$ as shown in the picture above.

e-5572.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
e-5572.problem:
Given the vector $\mathbf{x}$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system.
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/37beee87c5b5bd6350bd2c0f6353b61b1cfd321449a96b8b66aac99584d459bb.png)
e-5572.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:    

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, $x_3$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get $x_2=4x_3.$ 
Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain  

$$
x_1+4x_3+4x_3= 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-8x_3.
$$

So, the general solution is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/4995b9959cbb8a412fe0ed6198bfa9a82bcda40cd388c4759589e060ec16de1e.png)
Consequently, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/232c58060c7ba67f66564e8f8667fe67a84f6ef886a1c56e2d042224ace9b4db.png) is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-10)\cdot (-8)+20\cdot 4+2\cdot 1}{{(-8)}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{80+80+2}{64+16+1}b \\  & =\frac{162}{81}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}-8 \\ 4 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-16 \\ 8 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The projection is (a·b)/(a·a) times a. Since a·b = 12 − 30 + 24 = 6 and a·a = 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, the projection is 2a = [2, −2, 0, 2]ᵀ.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Let $b=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 30 \\ 12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto $\text{Span}{a}.$
after.worked_solution:
The vector projection of $b$ onto $\text{Span}{a}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 12+(-1)\cdot 30+0\cdot 12+1\cdot 24}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{12-30+0+24}{1+1+0+1}a \\  & =\frac{6}{3}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
content.problem: Let $b=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 30 \\ 12 \\ 24\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $b$ onto $\text{Span}{a}.$
content.worked_solution:
The vector projection of $b$ onto $\text{Span}{a}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,b & =\frac{a\cdot b}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 12+(-1)\cdot 30+0\cdot 12+1\cdot 24}{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{12-30+0+24}{1+1+0+1}a \\  & =\frac{6}{3}a \\  & =2a \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Let a=[2−48−6] and b=[213−1]. Find the orthogonal projection of a onto Span{b}.

a
[12−13]
b
[2−48−6]
c
[1−264]
d
[426−2]
e
[1−24−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: The projection is (b·a)/(b·b) times b. Here b·a = 4 − 4 + 24 + 6 = 30 and b·b = 4 + 1 + 9 + 1 = 15. Thus the projection is 2b = [4, 2, 6, −2]ᵀ.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 8 \\ -6\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2+1\cdot (-4)+3\cdot 8+(-1)\cdot (-6)}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{4+(-4)+24+6}{4+1+9+1}b \\  & =\frac{30}{15}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
content.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 8 \\ -6\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
content.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 2+1\cdot (-4)+3\cdot 8+(-1)\cdot (-6)}{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{4+(-4)+24+6}{4+1+9+1}b \\  & =\frac{30}{15}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ 6 \\ -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 2+1\cdot 2+0\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 5}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{2+2+0+5}{1+1+0+1}b \\  & =\frac{9}{3}b \\  & =3b \\  & =3[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ 0 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

Question 4
?

Let a=[12−34] and b=[42−31]. Find the orthogonal projection of a onto Span{b}.

a

b
[5475−25710]
c
[211075−2110145]

[1−32212]
e
[21−32]
Submit

decision.explanation: The projection is (b·a)/(b·b) times b. Here b·a = 4 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 21 and b·b = 16 + 4 + 9 + 1 = 30. Thus the projection is (7/10)b = [14/5, 7/5, −21/10, 7/10]ᵀ.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{4\cdot 1+2\cdot 2+(-3)\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 4}{{4}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{4+4+9+4}{16+4+9+1}b \\  & =\frac{21}{30}b \\  & =\frac{7}{10}b \\  & =\frac{7}{10}[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{14}{5} \\ \frac{7}{5} \\ -\frac{21}{10} \\ \frac{7}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
content.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
content.worked_solution:

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 10 \\ 6\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 8+1\cdot 4+(-1)\cdot 10+2\cdot 6}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{8+4-10+12}{1+1+1+4}b \\  & =\frac{14}{7}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto a One-Dimensional Subspace
content.problem: Let $a=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 10 \\ 6\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Find the orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$
content.worked_solution:
The orthogonal projection of $a$ onto $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{b\cdot a}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 8+1\cdot 4+(-1)\cdot 10+2\cdot 6}{{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{2}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{8+4-10+12}{1+1+1+4}b \\  & =\frac{14}{7}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ -2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]$ and $b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$ Find the distance between $x$ and $\text{Span}{b}.$
after.worked_solution:
The distance between the vector $x$ and the vector space $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by $‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖$, where $\overset{^}{x}$ in the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{span}{b}.$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{b\cdot x}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+0\cdot (-4)+(-3)\cdot (-2)+0\cdot 3}{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{6+0+6+0}{9+0+9+0}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-2)^{2}+((-4)-0)^{2}+((-2)-(-2))^{2}+(3-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+16+0+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

history.worked_solution:
The distance between the vector $x$ and the vector space $\text{Span}{b}$ is given by $‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖$, where $\overset{^}{x}$ in the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{span}{b}.$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{b}.$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{b\cdot x}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 2+0\cdot (-4)+(-3)\cdot (-2)+0\cdot 3}{{3}^{2}+{0}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{0}^{2}}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{6+0+6+0}{9+0+9+0}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\text{ }\,b \\  & =\frac{2}{3}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=\overset{^}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}‖x-\overset{^}{x}‖ & =\sqrt{({x}_{1}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{1})^{2}+({x}_{2}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{2})^{2}+({x}_{3}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{3})^{2}+({x}_{4}-{\overset{^}{x}}_{4})^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(2-2)^{2}+((-4)-0)^{2}+((-2)-(-2))^{2}+(3-0)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{0+16+0+9} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 6+3\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 6}{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+9+9+6}{1+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{30}{20}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:  

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].$

content.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 6+3\cdot 3+(-3)\cdot (-3)+1\cdot 6}{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{6+9+9+6}{1+9+9+1}a \\  & =\frac{30}{20}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following:  

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 3 \\ -3 \\ 6\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{9}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{3}{2} \\ \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}].$

after.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-5)+6\cdot 5+(-2)\cdot (-3)+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{-10+30+6+4}{4+36+4+16}a \\  & =\frac{30}{60}a \\  & =\frac{1}{2}a \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

content.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
content.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot (-5)+6\cdot 5+(-2)\cdot (-3)+4\cdot 1}{{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{4}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{-10+30+6+4}{4+36+4+16}a \\  & =\frac{30}{60}a \\  & =\frac{1}{2}a \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 5 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}-6 \\ 2 \\ -2 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

after.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 12+6\cdot 6+(-6)\cdot (-6)+2\cdot 12}{{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+{2}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{24+36+36+24}{4+36+36+4}a \\  & =\frac{120}{80}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{2\cdot 12+6\cdot 6+(-6)\cdot (-6)+2\cdot 12}{{2}^{2}+{6}^{2}+(-6)^{2}+{2}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{24+36+36+24}{4+36+36+4}a \\  & =\frac{120}{80}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}a \\  & =\frac{3}{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 6 \\ -6 \\ 12\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 9 \\ -9 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ -3 \\ 3 \\ 9\end{aligned}].$

after.problem: Let $x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]$ and $a=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ If $x=y+z,$ where $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ then $z=$
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14066555/assets/d887852fe51f08cb7296437e69b6a9632721cfd155558e6abf9a99b4f59f7ad6.png)

First, we find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $\text{Span}{a}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x & =\frac{a\cdot x}{a\cdot a}a \\  & =\frac{1\cdot 3+2\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 2+3\cdot 4}{{1}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}}a \\  & =\frac{3+2+(-2)+12}{1+4+1+9}a \\  & =\frac{15}{15}a \\  & =a \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the following: 

$$
\begin{aligned}y & ={\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ z & =x-{\text{proj}}_{a}\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that $y\in \text{Span}{a}$ and $z⊥\text{Span}{a},$ as shown in the picture above.

In conclusion, $z=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

decision.explanation: The equations give x₂ = −x₁ and x₃ = −x₁, so the solution space is spanned by b = [−1, 1, 1]ᵀ. For the given vector, x·b = 2 + 3 + 7 = 12 and b·b = 3. Hence the projection is 4b = [−4, 4, 4]ᵀ.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1+7\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{12}{3}b \\  & =4b \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ 7\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{(-2)\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1+7\cdot 1}{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{12}{3}b \\  & =4b \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 4 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & \frac{1}{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}+3\cdot 1}{{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{5}{\frac{1}{4}+1}b \\  & =4b \\  & =4[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system.

Consider the augmented matrix M of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

M=[2−10−1120]R2:=R2+12R1∼[2−10000].

In the reduced matrix above, there is 1 pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we get x1=12x2. So, the general solution is [12x2x2]=x2[121],x2∈R.

Consequently, B={[121]} is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of x onto the solution space of the system: projbx=x⋅bb⋅bb=4⋅12+3⋅1(12)2+12b=514+1b=4b=4[121]=[24]

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 5 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}-8{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & -5 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -8 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=2{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
{x}_{1}-3\cdot (2{x}_{3})=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=6{x}_{3}.
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}6{x}_{3} \\ 2{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{12\cdot 6+5\cdot 2+0\cdot 1}{{6}^{2}+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{82}{41}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ 4 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector onto the Solution Space of a System of Equations
content.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}11 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis of the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there is $1$ pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=-{x}_{2}.$ So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]={x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{11\cdot (-1)+3\cdot 1}{{(-1)}^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{-8}{2}b \\  & =-4b \\  & =-4[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The equations give x₁ = x₃ and x₂ = −3x₃, so the solution space is spanned by b = [1, −3, 1]ᵀ. Since x·b = 3 + 15 + 4 = 22 and b·b = 11, the projection is 2b = [2, −6, 2]ᵀ.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Given the vector $x$ and the system of linear equations below, find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system.

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we need to find a basis for the solution space of the system. 

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system, which we reduce to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}$ and from the second equation ${x}_{2}=-3{x}_{3}.$  

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-3)+4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{22}{11}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are $2$ pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. Now, from the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}$ and from the second equation ${x}_{2}=-3{x}_{3}.$  

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ -3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Consequently, $B={[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of the solution space of the system.

Finally, we find the projection of $x$ onto the solution space of the system:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{b}\,x & =\frac{x\cdot b}{b\cdot b}b \\  & =\frac{3\cdot 1+(-5)\cdot (-3)+4\cdot 1}{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}b \\  & =\frac{22}{11}b \\  & =2b \\  & =2[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
